summary: This specification describes how to configure proactive MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) OAM functions for a Label Switched Path using TLVs carried by the GMPLS RSVP-TE protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to set up the built-in health checks on a network path at the same time as the path itself is created.

subtitle: How to switch on MPLS-TP health checks, loss and delay measurement, and fault signals while a path is being set up.

tldr.problem: Transport networks need health monitoring on each Label Switched Path, but configuring it separately on every node by hand is slow and error prone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of sub-TLVs, carried in GMPLS RSVP-TE signaling, that configure BFD continuity checks, loss and delay measurement, and fault management signals at the same time the path is established.
tldr.outcome: Operators can bring up an LSP with its proactive OAM already running, and nodes that cannot honor a requested setting report a specific OAM Problem error.

today: RFC 7487 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7260, which supplies the generic OAM configuration framework.

sections.title: Configuring OAM Along with the Path
sections.content:
RFC 7487 describes how to configure proactive MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) OAM functions for a given Label Switched Path (LSP), using TLVs carried by GMPLS RSVP-TE (RFC 3473). RFC 7260 already defines how RSVP-TE configures OAM in a technology-agnostic way. This document adds the pieces specific to MPLS-TP: information elements and procedures for the OAM running between Label Edge Routers (LERs).

On-demand OAM is out of scope. The RFC expects on-demand functions to be started by reaching the network nodes directly through a management interface.

Because MPLS-TP must be able to operate without a control plane (RFC 5654), RSVP-TE is only one option. The RFC lists a Network Management System, LSP Ping and RSVP-TE as ways to configure the same OAM.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a network path and its health checks used to be two jobs. This RFC lets you do both in one go.

sections.title: The OAM Functions Being Configured
sections.content:
Proactive MPLS-TP OAM is built from existing protocols, and this RFC only configures them:

  • BFD (RFC 6428) for Continuity Check and Connectivity Verification. It has a "CC mode" with symmetric timers and a "CV/CC mode" that also sends unique maintenance entity identifiers.
  • Loss Measurement and Delay Measurement (RFC 6374) for packet loss, throughput, delay and jitter.
  • Fault Management Signals (RFC 6427): Alarm Indication Signal (AIS), Link Down Indication (LDI) and Lock Report (LKR), which let a server LSP tell client LSPs about faults.

Some consequent actions of defects such as Loss Of Continuity can also be operator-configured, for example whether a LOC defect blocks outgoing data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of checks: "are you still there?", "how fast and how lossy is the road?", and "warning, something upstream broke!". The RFC only says how to turn them on.

sections.title: How the Configuration Is Signaled
sections.content:
GMPLS RSVP-TE, or alternatively LSP Ping, can simply enable OAM functions by setting flags in the OAM Function Flags Sub-TLV from RFC 7260. For finer control, you add sub-TLVs for each function. This RFC adds a new OAM type, MPLS OAM (3), and a container called the MPLS OAM Configuration Sub-TLV (type 33).

Intermediate nodes SHOULD NOT process or modify the OAM Configuration TLVs and just forward them to the end node. The exception is the MPLS OAM FMS Sub-TLV, which MUST be examined even by supporting intermediate nodes, but acted on only by nodes able to transmit FMS signals into the LSP.

The container has some general rules:

  • It MAY be empty; its Length is then 8, and every function with its flag set gets default values or is left disabled.
  • A sub-TLV without a matching flag MUST be silently ignored.
  • If a sub-TLV appears more than once, only the first is used.

If the sub-TLV is placed in LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES and a node supports RFC 7260 but not the FMS sub-TLV, it MUST send a PathErr with "OAM Problem/Configuration Error". In LSP_ATTRIBUTES, unsupporting nodes forward the message without an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup message carries a little checklist. Routers in the middle mostly pass it along, and only the router at the end of the path reads most of it.

sections.title: BFD Continuity Configuration
sections.content:
The BFD Configuration Sub-TLV (type 1) MUST be included when the CC flag, the CV flag, or both are set. It carries version and flag bits and then its own sub-TLVs. Key flags are N (timer negotiation through BFD Control messages), S (symmetric timing), I (integrity), G and U (BFD carried in the G-ACh or in UDP; G wins if both are set) and B (bidirectional versus unidirectional mode).

BFD MUST run either in asynchronous mode, with both sides active, or in unidirectional mode. The simplest scenario uses RSVP-TE only to bootstrap a BFD session with no timer negotiation.

The nested sub-TLVs are:

  • BFD Identifiers (type 1, length 20): a non-zero Local Discriminator plus MPLS-TP Global_ID, Node Identifier, Tunnel_Num and LSP_Num. It MUST always be included, because the ingress cannot know the egress's locally assigned Tunnel ID.
  • Negotiation Timer Parameters (type 2, length 16): transmit and receive intervals in microseconds, and the Echo interval. Required when the N flag is cleared.
  • BFD Authentication (type 3, length 8): the Auth Type and Auth Key ID. Key exchange is out of scope.
  • Traffic Class (type 4): the TC value to use in the MPLS label stack entry, otherwise a local decision.

BFD Control packets in the G-ACh have no end-to-end checksum, so a single flipped bit could make the far end wrongly conclude the link is down. Setting the Integrity flag enables Keyed SHA1 with an empty key (all 0s), so each packet carries a hash that detects errors. If a real pre-shared key is wanted, the BFD Authentication Sub-TLV MUST be included.

If the CV flag is set, the CC flag MUST be set too, since connectivity verification implies a continuity check. The CV/CC message then contains the LSP MEP-ID.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD is like two friends tapping each other every so often to say "still here". The setup says how often to tap and how to check that a tap was not garbled on the way.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring and Fault Signals
sections.content:
The Performance Monitoring Sub-TLV (type 2) MUST be present when the PM/Loss, PM/Delay or PM/Throughput flag is set. Its flags choose direct or inferred delay (D) and loss (L), and switch on jitter (J), dyadic (Y), loopback (K) and combined (C) modes. It can hold two sub-TLVs, used only when defaults are not wanted.

  • MPLS OAM PM Loss (length 20): origin timestamp format (default IEEE 1588 version 1), traffic-class (T) and octet-count (B) flags, a Measurement Interval (default 100 milliseconds), a Test Interval (default 10 milliseconds) and a Loss Threshold.
  • MPLS OAM PM Delay (length 20): the same layout, with a default Measurement Interval of 1000 milliseconds, a default Test Interval of 10 milliseconds, and a Delay Threshold in milliseconds for two-way delay.

Throughput uses the same tool as loss measurement, so the Loss sub-TLV serves both.

The MPLS OAM FMS Sub-TLV (type 3) configures fault signals. The E flag enables AIS and LKR signaling (default 1), the S flag asks a server MEP to transmit AIS and LKR on client LSPs (default 0), and the T flag marks that a timer value is set (default 0). The Refresh Timer MUST be between 1 and 20 seconds. When working and protection paths are both signaled, they SHOULD use identical E, T and refresh timer settings.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides "still here?", you can ask the path to time how long messages take and count how many go missing, and to shout a warning to other paths when something breaks.

sections.title: Errors and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
An egress node that cannot honor a requested setting MUST generate a specific error under the "OAM Problem" error code from RFC 7260. The RFC assigns sub-codes 13 through 25, for example Unsupported BFD Version (13), Unsupported BFD Authentication Type (15), Unsupported Delay Mode (18), Fault management signaling unsupported (24) and Unable to create fault management association (25). Missing required sub-TLVs produce "OAM Problem/Configuration Error".

IANA allocated the MPLS OAM type (3) and the MPLS OAM Configuration Sub-TLV (33) in the RSVP-TE OAM Configuration Registry. It also created sub-registries for the BFD and Performance Monitoring sub-TLV types and for the MPLS OAM Configuration Sub-TLV types, with new values allocated through IETF Review except for a range reserved for experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: If the router at the end cannot do something you asked for, it sends back a numbered note saying exactly which thing it could not do.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Signaling OAM parameters and automatically creating OAM entities adds security considerations beyond those of RFC 3473. The main one named is overload: an attacker could request high-frequency liveliness monitoring of a large number of LSPs, targeting a single network element. The RFC points to RFC 7260 and RFC 6060 for this, and to RFC 5920 for wider MPLS and GMPLS security discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad guy could ask one router to run thousands of check-ups per second until it is too busy to do its real job.
